subtype: Working overly hard to avoid exposure [Actor]
passage: In her first month at the consultancy in Madrid, Layla was always the last to leave. She rehearsed every meeting, rechecked every chart three times, and wrote answers to questions nobody would ask. When her first client presentation went well, Diego, who'd joined with her, said, "You were brilliant." Layla shook her head. "Only because I prepared for eleven hours. If I hadn't, they'd have seen I don't know anything." She felt a wave of relief at having got away with it, and a knot of fear about the next one. Diego frowned. "You've done that for every meeting. Has one ever gone badly?" Layla thought. None had. "That's because I overprepared," she said. Diego sighed. "Or because you're good."

qa.q: How long did Layla prepare for her first client presentation?
qa.a: Eleven hours.

qa.q: Why did Layla feel relief and fear at the same time after the presentation?
qa.a: Relief that she hadn't been exposed, and fear because she credits the success to overwork, so the next meeting feels just as dangerous.

qa.q: What small experiment could help Layla test her belief?
qa.a: Preparing a normal amount for one low-stakes meeting and seeing how it goes, so a success can't be credited only to overwork.

qa.q: How does Diego see Layla's success differently?
qa.a: Diego sees a string of good meetings as evidence that she is good, not just over-prepared, and is frustrated she won't believe it.

grounding: A new employee over-prepares to avoid being exposed, and credits every success to overwork.

subtype: Working overly hard to avoid exposure [Actor]
passage: At the bank's head office in Chennai, the cleaning staff knew Yamini by name; she was still at her desk when they came at nine. Four months into her first job as a credit analyst, she read every file twice and wrote notes for meetings she might not even be called into. When Vaibhav, her team lead, praised her risk report in front of everyone, she smiled, then went to the washroom and stood there, breathing. It had worked, but only because she'd stayed till eleven all week, she told herself. Next time it might not. Vaibhav found her at her desk again that night. "Yamini, you're one of the sharpest people on this team," he said. "Would you believe that if you'd left at six?" She didn't answer. She didn't know.

qa.q: Who knew Yamini by name at the head office?
qa.a: The cleaning staff.

qa.q: Why did Yamini go to the washroom and stand there breathing after the praise?
qa.a: The praise brought relief mixed with fear; she felt she had only escaped exposure through overwork and worried the next report would reveal her.

qa.q: Which question from Vaibhav points to a way out?
qa.a: "Would you believe that if you'd left at six?", which invites her to test whether her skill, not the late nights, produces good work.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel finding Yamini at her desk again at night?
qa.a: Vaibhav is likely concerned, seeing a strong analyst wearing herself out because she doesn't trust her own ability.

grounding: A new analyst works late and over-prepares to avoid being found unqualified, and credits praise to overwork.

subtype: Working overly hard to avoid exposure [Actor]
passage:
Dear Tejas,
You asked how the new job is going. On paper, great: the head of department says my Class 8 lessons are the best planned in the school. What I haven't told anyone is how. I stay till eight most nights. I write out every word I'll say. I prepare three backup activities for each period in case a child asks something I can't answer. And every time a lesson goes well, I feel this rush of relief, as if I've escaped being found out. Then the fear starts again for tomorrow. Last week I had a fever and taught from a rough outline, and the lesson went fine. That scared me more, somehow. I don't know what I'm proving, or to whom. Write back?
Vinita

qa.q: How many backup activities does Vinita prepare for each period?
qa.a: Three backup activities.

qa.q: Why did the lesson taught from a rough outline scare Vinita?
qa.a: It showed that the overwork might not be what makes lessons good, which shakes the belief that effort alone is hiding a lack of skill.

qa.q: What choice could Vinita try, based on the fever day?
qa.a: Deliberately teaching one lesson a week from a lighter outline, so success can be credited to real skill rather than to late nights.

qa.q: How might Tejas respond to this letter?
qa.a: Tejas may feel concerned about the long nights and point out that the fever-day lesson is evidence of ability, not luck.

grounding: A new teacher over-prepares every lesson for fear of being found out, and credits success to the overwork.

subtype: Working overly hard to avoid exposure [Actor]
passage: Mridul, you asked why I'm never at the Friday dinners. Okay, the real reason. I joined the audit firm in June and I'm terrified they'll figure out I don't know enough. So I stay till ten every night. I prepare notes for meetings I'm not even invited to. I read every past file twice. Last month my manager said my report was the best from the new batch, and for about an hour I felt amazing. Relief, basically. Then I thought, that's only because I worked till midnight all week. If I ever stop, they'll see. So I worked till midnight the next week too. It's like proving it all over again every day, and it never sticks. I'm Eshaan, I'm tired, and I still don't believe I'm good at this.

qa.q: Until what time does Eshaan stay at the office every night?
qa.a: Eshaan stays till ten every night.

qa.q: Why doesn't the manager's praise last for Eshaan?
qa.a: Eshaan credits the good report to overwork, not ability, so the relief fades and the fear of exposure returns, demanding even more hours.

qa.q: What choice could break the cycle for Eshaan?
qa.a: Leaving on time for one week on a normal report and seeing how it's received; if it's still good, that is evidence the skill, not the overwork, carries the work.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel hearing 'I'm tired'?
qa.a: Mridul would likely feel worried and glad to be trusted with the truth, and may want to gently pull Eshaan back to the Friday dinners.

grounding: A new employee overworks out of fear of being seen as unqualified and credits every success to the extra hours.

subtype: Working overly hard to avoid exposure [Actor]
passage: I'm Farhan, and I sit opposite Ganga at the civil engineering firm. She joined in April, straight out of college. Her drawings are clean; her calculations rarely need checking. Yet she's the last to leave every night, lights off except her desk lamp. She brings three versions of every sketch to reviews, "just in case". When the director praised her bridge-load report, she said, "I just put in a lot of hours," and went straight back to work. One night I asked why she stayed so late. She laughed a bit too fast. "If I leave at six, someone will find the mistake I missed." I can't know everything she feels, but it looks as if the more she overworks, the more convinced she is that overwork is all she's got.

qa.q: How many versions of every sketch does Ganga bring to reviews?
qa.a: Three versions.

qa.q: What does Ganga's too-fast laugh suggest?
qa.a: She seems anxious and a little embarrassed, afraid that leaving at six would expose her, and uneasy admitting it.

qa.q: What could Farhan say or do that might help Ganga see her real skill?
qa.a: Point out specifically that her calculations rarely need checking and that the report was praised for its content, and suggest trying one review with a single version.

qa.q: How does Ganga's pattern look from Farhan's desk?
qa.a: To Farhan it looks like a trap: every success gets credited to the late hours, which only deepens her belief that overwork is all she has.

grounding: A colleague sees a capable new engineer over-prepare and stay late out of fear, crediting her success to overwork.
